fixes.explanation: Opens and repairs, exactly right. It's the first month of his first year, and Hezekiah is already working on the doors of the house of the LORD. I think a king who fixes the doors wants that house open again. He doesn't even wait for his second month, friend.
Verse 3 says he opened and repaired the doors. Taking them down isn't what the text says. Think repair crew with a toolbox, not a moving truck. So the answer is opens and repairs them.

Impurity is the word. Hezekiah tells the Levites to consecrate themselves and the house of the LORD, and to remove from the Holy Place every impurity. Notice he starts with the Levites themselves, friend. The cleaners get ready too.

Offerings do come up in his speech, but as something the fathers didn't do. Hezekiah says they did not "…present burnt offerings in the Holy Place of the God of Israel." (2 Chronicles 29:7) The thing he tells the Levites to remove is every impurity. So the blank is impurity.
True. Hezekiah tells the Levites the wrath of the LORD has fallen upon Judah and Jerusalem. He adds, "…as you can see with your own eyes." It's a serious line, friend.

A covenant with the LORD, yes. Hezekiah says it is in his heart to make one so that His fierce anger will turn away from them. That covenant is with the LORD, the God of Israel. That's a good place for a king's heart to be.
Gifts to the king of Assyria don't appear in this speech. What's in Hezekiah's heart is a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel. He says it's so that His fierce anger will turn away from them.

Leading an army out against Edom isn't what verse 10 says. Hezekiah says what's in his heart is a covenant with the LORD, the God of Israel. He wants it so that His fierce anger will turn away from them. So the answer is the covenant, friend.
The elders will have to sit this verse out, friend. They don't appear in it. The command came from the king, and it went by the words of the LORD. So the blank holds king.

The Valley of Elah is where David faced Goliath (1 Samuel 17:2–50). Famous place, but not the one in this verse. The Levites carry the unclean things out to the Kidron Valley. Different valley, friend.

Twenty sounds like the round number a contractor would quote you, friend. But the text counts it out: day eight at the portico, then eight more days on the house itself. They finish on the sixteenth day of the first month. Sixteen is the number.

The report says the opposite. The Levites tell Hezekiah they prepared and consecrated all the articles King Ahaz in his unfaithfulness cast aside. Those articles are now in front of the altar of the LORD. So the answer is True, and the things that were cast aside have been made ready.
Oil isn't what the text says here. In this verse the priests take the blood and splatter it on the altar, animal after animal. Bulls, then rams, then lambs. The blank is blood, friend.

Trumpets. The Levites stand with the instruments of David, and the priests with the trumpets. Add the cymbals, harps and lyres the Levites have been given (2 Chronicles 29:25), and that's a lot of music in one house. I'd have wanted a front row seat for that sound check.
They bow down and worship. When the offerings are completed, the king and all those present with him do exactly that. The king is right there with everyone else. That's worship from the whole crowd.

Heading back to the palace isn't what the verse says. When the offerings are completed, the king and all those present with him bow down and worship. Worship is the next thing the text gives us, friend.

Hearts. The verse says "…all whose hearts were willing brought burnt offerings." The assembly also brings sacrifices and thank offerings. So the ones bringing burnt offerings are the willing ones, friend.
Benjamites don't appear in this verse. The helpers are the priests' Levite brothers, and they help until the work is finished. The blank is Levite, friend.
Ephraimites aren't brought in here. The ones who help the priests are their Levite brothers. They help until the work is finished, friend.
